tldr: SoRoMoX is an open-source framework that implements reduced-order soft robot models based on Cosserat-rod theory in JAX, enabling fast GPU-parallel simulation, end-to-end automatic differentiation, and unified access to dynamics terms essential for control.
hero_caption: Overview of SoRoMoX. It handles articulated and continuum (PCS/GVS) soft robot models under a unified interface, leveraging JAX's JIT compilation, automatic differentiation, and GPU parallelization to seamlessly support system identification, model predictive control, reinforcement learning, and safety-constrained control.
overview:
In rigid-body robotics, simulators supporting GPU parallelization and automatic differentiation—such as MuJoCo XLA and Isaac Gym—have emerged, making large-scale reinforcement learning and trajectory optimization standard practice. In contrast, for the control and system identification of continuously deformable soft robots, a major gap has remained: despite well-established theoretical reduced-order models based on Cosserat-rod theory, existing implementations are largely confined to MATLAB-based CPU computation, lack automatic differentiation and GPU parallelization, and cannot be integrated into advanced computational pipelines.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed SoRoMoX (Soft Robot Models in JAX), a fully numerical, JIT-compilable Python/JAX soft robot modeling framework. SoRoMoX uniformly handles continuum models—including Piecewise Constant Strain (PCS) and Geometric Variable Strain (GVS)—as well as articulated flexible models, directly providing inertia matrices, Coriolis terms, elastic and gravitational forces, and Jacobians tailored for control algorithms.

In benchmarks, SoRoMoX achieves up to an 18.1× speedup in sequential execution compared to the existing CPU library (SoRoSim), and up to a 234.6× throughput improvement through batched GPU-parallel simulation.

Thanks to this extraordinary computational efficiency and differentiability, the authors demonstrated six advanced application case studies previously impractical or impossible for soft robots: high-accuracy physical parameter identification from static-equilibrium data (66% error reduction), residual-force learning, computed-torque control (error reduced by a factor of approximately 500), automatic gain optimization via differentiable rollouts, contact force safety constraints via high-order control barrier functions (HOCBF, keeping peak contact force within 5 N instead of 33.5 N), and 7× faster reinforcement learning via GPU parallelization—successfully raising the baseline of soft-robot control implementation.
contributions: Integrated and implemented Cosserat-rod-based reduced-order soft robot models (PCS, GVS) and articulated flexible models in a GPU-native, fully differentiable form using JAX for the first time.

Provided a comprehensive, control-ready unified API for essential dynamics terms—such as inertia matrices, gravity and elastic forces, Jacobians, and spatial transformations—rather than treating simulation as a black box.
Achieved up to an 18.1× speedup in sequential CPU computation over existing SoRoSim, and up to a 234.6× simulation throughput improvement through batched GPU parallelization.

Demonstrated six advanced control and learning pipelines enabled by high speed and differentiability: system identification, residual learning, computed-torque control, gain optimization, HOCBF contact force safety control, and parallel reinforcement learning.

sections.heading: Breaking through the computational implementation bottleneck in soft robotics
sections.summary: Although soft robot control theory has matured, the lack of GPU parallelization and automatic differentiation in implementation frameworks has been a primary bottleneck. SoRoMoX resolves this using JAX, bringing the modern optimization and learning workflows common in rigid robotics to soft robots.
sections.details:
Soft robots possess remarkable physical intelligence, adapting naturally to their environments through continuous compliance. However, handling continuous deformation with infinite degrees of freedom has long posed a fundamental challenge. Over the past decade, reduced-order modeling based on Cosserat-rod theory has progressed significantly by projecting strain fields onto finite coordinate representations—notably Piecewise Constant Strain (PCS) and Geometric Variable Strain (GVS)—solidifying the theoretical modeling foundation.

Nevertheless, the bottleneck has shifted from model derivation to computational deployment. Rigid-body robotics enjoys tools like MuJoCo XLA (MJX) and JaxSim, which run tens of thousands of parallel rollouts on GPUs and leverage automatic differentiation for fast trajectory optimization and reinforcement learning. In contrast, existing soft robot tools (such as MATLAB-based SoRoSim or CPU-based PyElastica) either lack automatic differentiation, do not expose internal model structures (inertia matrices, Jacobians, etc.) to controllers, or cannot take advantage of modern GPU accelerators.

The proposed framework, SoRoMoX, is an open-source Python/JAX framework for soft robots. It fully supports fast JIT-compiled single-model evaluation, massive batched evaluation on GPUs/TPUs, and end-to-end automatic differentiation with respect to states, inputs, and parameters. This directly brings the powerful computational machinery of rigid robotics into the domain of soft robots.

sections.heading: Unifying rigid to continuum systems with a control-ready API
sections.summary: SoRoMoX supports articulated soft robots and continuum rod models (PCS/GVS), exposing equations of motion components and Jacobians under a unified interface for control. It also includes model-based controllers and versatile visualization tools.
sections.details:
SoRoMoX provides features structured into four key areas: model representations, a control-oriented interface, controllers, and visualization.

- II-A Model Families
SoRoMoX supports two primary families. The first is ArticulatedSoftRobot, covering rigid links combined with flexible joints, elastic tendons, or pneumatic artificial muscles (such as McKibben actuators). The second is Continuum Soft Robots, which represent continuous deformation with a small set of strain coordinates based on Cosserat-rod theory. It supports both PCS (2D and 3D), assuming constant strain along each segment, and GVS, representing strain fields as superpositions of spatial basis functions. PCS leverages analytical closed-form kinematics for extreme computational efficiency, while GVS captures complex bending and torsion with high fidelity.

- II-B A Control-Ready Model Interface
The core philosophy of SoRoMoX is that models must not simply be black-box simulators. Downstream control and optimization require direct access not only to forward kinematics $g(q,s)$ and Jacobians $J(q,s)$, but also to the individual dynamic terms: the inertia matrix $M(q)$, Coriolis/centrifugal terms $C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q}$, gravity forces $G(q)$, elastic forces $K(q)$, damping terms $D\dot{q}$, and the actuation matrix $A(q)$. SoRoMoX exposes all of these through a unified API, accompanied by built-in coordinate transformation tools for operational space and actuation space dynamics.

- II-C & II-D Model-Based Controllers & Extensibility
Leveraging these model terms, standard controllers are bundled into the framework: PID, gravity/potential compensation, feedforward compensation, computed-torque (CT) control, and operational space impedance control. Implemented as type-safe JAX/Equinox objects, adding custom robots is as simple as subclassing the base class and specifying cross-section geometries or tendon routings.

- II-E Rendering and Visualization
To inspect soft robot behaviors, a unified interface flexibly switches between lightweight Matplotlib plotting, Open3D-based 3D mesh rendering, and browser-based real-time visualization or video recording via Viser.

sections.heading: From simulation to differentiable optimization in just a few lines of code
sections.summary: Designed with an intuitive Python API, SoRoMoX uses typed definitions separating parameters from static structure. It integrates smoothly with Diffrax for differentiable ODE integration and standard JAX primitives like JIT, vmap, and grad.
sections.details:
SoRoMoX requires Python 3.10+ and installs straightforwardly via `pip install soromox`. Its code architecture is carefully designed to balance user convenience with high computational throughput.

- III-A & III-B API Overview and Differentiable Workflows
Model definitions strictly separate dynamic parameters (numerical values like geometry, material properties, and Young's modulus) stored in a "parameter PyTree" from static structure (array shapes, basis function degrees, etc.). As a result, updating parameters and re-evaluating avoids triggering JAX recompilation, enabling extremely fast gradient-based optimization loops.

Simulation uses Diffrax, the ODE solver library in the JAX ecosystem, defaulting to high-precision Tsit5 (Tsitouras 5/4 method) integration. Users can set up continuous-time closed-loop rollouts as well as zero-order hold (ZOH) discrete sampled-data control simulations in just a few lines of code.

Furthermore, because all function calls are fully JAX-compatible, users can apply `jax.jit` for blistering execution speed, `jax.vmap` for batching across environments, and `jax.grad` or `jax.jacrev` to obtain derivatives of robot behavior in a single line. This makes physical system identification and control gain tuning through gradient descent remarkably streamlined.

sections.heading: Up to 18x faster on CPU and 235x faster with GPU parallelization
sections.summary: Computational speed and accuracy were benchmarked against leading libraries (SoRoSim, PyElastica). SoRoMoX outperforms SoRoSim by up to 18.1× on a single CPU core and delivers up to a 234.6× throughput boost through GPU batch parallelization.
sections.details:
To evaluate SoRoMoX's performance, benchmark experiments were conducted using flexible beam deformation simulations. Baselines included SoRoSim (a MATLAB library implementing reduced-order models) and PyElastica (a fast C++/Python library solving discrete Cosserat rods analogous to finite elements).

- Sequential CPU Rollout Performance
Four scenarios simulating 3 seconds of behavior under external forces and tendon tensions were tested on a 0.6 m cylindrical beam. SoRoMoX reproduced virtually identical physics compared to SoRoSim (tip position RMSE between 0.86 mm and 7.21 mm, representing only 0.14% to 1.20% of the beam length) while delivering dramatic speedups.
Specifically, SoRoMoX achieved speedups of approximately 18.1× for planar PCS, 5.9× for spatial PCS, 1.5× for complex GVS, and 2.1× for tendon-driven GVS. While PyElastica can be faster in pure forward simulation alone, it cannot output dynamics matrices required for control (such as inertia or Coriolis matrices) nor support automatic differentiation, making SoRoMoX vastly superior as a control-oriented reduced-order modeling platform.

- GPU Batched Parallel Scaling
Next, batched simulation throughput was measured on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU using `jax.vmap` to run independent simulations concurrently. The authors evaluated how simulation throughput (the ratio of simulated physical time to wall-clock time) scaled as batch size $n_{\mathrm{b}}$ increased from 1 to 256.
For articulated soft robots, scaling maintained 79.5% to 91.6% of ideal linear scaling at batch size 256, achieving speedups of 203.6× to 234.6×. Continuum models also showed massive scaling: up to 196.2× for planar PCS, 155.6× for spatial PCS, and 175.4× for spatial GVS. At batch size 256, articulated and planar PCS systems, as well as multi-segment spatial PCS and GVS models, generated simulation data substantially faster than real time in aggregate throughput.

sections.heading: Six real-world pipelines: from system ID and control to safety and RL
sections.summary: The authors demonstrated six application case studies fully leveraging automatic differentiation and GPU parallelization: system identification, residual learning, model-based control, gain optimization, barrier-function safety control, and parallel reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
Six case studies demonstrate the capabilities of SoRoMoX:

- V-A & V-B Static Equilibrium System Identification and Residual Learning
Using experimental data from a physical tendon-driven conical soft arm (four motion-captured marker positions), three material parameters were identified: Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, and mass density. Because SoRoMoX expresses static equilibrium solving as a differentiable computation graph, gradient-based optimization reduced marker position root-mean-square error (RMSE) from 56.9 mm down to 19.3 mm (a 66% reduction). Combining this with residual-force learning—using a neural network to capture unmodeled friction and hysteresis—further reduced RMSE to 6.9 mm (an additional 64% reduction).

- V-C Model-Based Control
On a single-segment 3D PCS robot, model-free PD/PID control was compared against potential compensation (PC), feedforward compensation (FF), and computed-torque (CT) control. CT control, which uses exact dynamic model terms for feedback linearization, reduced tracking RMSE by approximately a factor of 500 relative to model-free PD control. Furthermore, operational space impedance control on a two-segment robot achieved highly accurate spherical figure-8 tracking with a tip position error of only 2.84 mm.

- V-D Control Gain Optimization
By differentiating through the entire closed-loop simulation, PID control gains were optimized directly via gradient descent. Compared to manually tuned baselines, this reduced the integrated tracking error loss by up to 62% and shortened settling time by 64%.

- V-E Safety-Constrained Control via High-Order Barrier Functions (HOCBF)
In a task requiring reaching a target pose while constraining contact force with an obstacle within 5 N, an unconstrained high-order control Lyapunov function (HOCLF) controller caused peak contact force to spike to 33.5 N. In contrast, incorporating an HOCBF using SoRoMoX's higher-order differentiable dynamics strictly bounded contact forces below 5 N while successfully converging toward the goal (reducing safety violation rate from 570% to 0%).

- V-F GPU-Parallel Reinforcement Learning
In a target-tracking task on a hemisphere, reinforcement learning was performed using the PPO algorithm. Leveraging GPU-parallel environments in SoRoMoX (with 256 or 512 parallel rollouts), policy training reached target performance up to 7× faster than a CPU-based PyElastica baseline. The trained policy achieved a 91.4% step success rate.

sections.heading: Toward a modern computational standard for soft-robot control and learning
sections.summary: SoRoMoX introduces a modern, high-speed, differentiable software stack to soft robotics. Future work includes accelerated planar GVS models, support for floating bases and branched kinematic trees, and broader smart actuation mechanisms.
sections.details:
SoRoMoX is the first open-source framework to unify reduced-order Cosserat-rod theory with modern GPU-parallel and automatic differentiation computing infrastructure. Going beyond pure simulation, it exposes the complete internal structure of the equations of motion required for controller design, opening up direct applications of powerful optimization and machine learning algorithms to soft robotics.

The authors outline several promising directions for future development:
- Implementing faster planar GVS environments for rapid algorithmic prototyping before scaling to spatial models
- Supporting floating bases (for mobile soft robots), branched kinematic trees, and closed-loop parallel mechanisms
- Expanding actuation support to smart materials beyond tendons and fluidics, such as shape memory alloys (SMA), dielectric elastomer actuators (DEA), and jamming mechanisms
- Assisting in the creation of standardized robot description formats (analogous to URDF in rigid robotics) to share soft robot models across different simulation tools

Released under the MIT license on GitHub, SoRoMoX is positioned to become a foundational shared infrastructure advancing future research in soft robotics.

sections.heading: Inside the architecture: what makes SoRoMoX fast and stably differentiable
sections.summary: The appendix details the internal design choices behind SoRoMoX's performance, including parameter-structure decoupling, custom JVPs for singularity avoidance and speed, and projection into operational and actuation spaces.
sections.details:
The appendix details the internal software architecture that gives SoRoMoX its computational speed, numerical stability, and parallel efficiency.

- Decoupling Parameters from Structure (Appendix A-A)
Static structural properties (array shapes, quadrature integration point counts, actuator routing topologies) are strictly isolated from dynamic parameters (Young's modulus, mass density, etc.). Because parameter updates do not trigger JAX recompilations, updating models within optimization loops is exceptionally lightweight.

- Analytic Differentiation Hooks and Custom JVPs (Appendix A-C)
Relying naively on automatic differentiation for every operation can lead to bloated computational graphs, memory pressure, and performance degradation. SoRoMoX defines custom Jacobian-Vector Products (JVPs) where analytic closed forms are known—such as time derivatives of Jacobians $\dot{J}$ and strain energy gradients—ensuring the differentiation engine directly evaluates efficient analytical expressions.

- Operational and Actuation Space Projections (Appendix A-D)
For task-space control, SoRoMoX provides routines to compute the operational space inertia matrix $\Lambda(q) = (J M^{-1} J^\top)^{-1}$ and dynamically consistent generalized inverses. Furthermore, for underactuated tendon-driven systems, an `ActuationSpaceDynamics` abstraction projects equations of motion into actuated and unactuated coordinates via QR decomposition, facilitating the construction of advanced nonlinear controllers.

- Efficient Spatial Quadrature Implementation (Appendix E-A)
Serial spatial dependencies from root to tip are evaluated using `jax.lax.scan`, while independent calculations across Gauss quadrature points within each segment are vectorized with `jax.vmap`. This avoids symbolic expression expansion while extracting maximum execution performance on GPUs.

takeaways: Reduced-order Cosserat-rod models now possess rigid-robotics-grade GPU parallelization and end-to-end differentiability through JAX.
Direct API access to underlying dynamics terms (inertia matrices, elastic forces, Jacobians) rather than treating simulations as black boxes directly accelerates model-based controller design.
Differentiating through static equilibrium solutions and full closed-loop simulations drastically simplifies parameter identification and automatic gain tuning.
Combining high-order control barrier functions (HOCBF) with exact second-order differentiable dynamics provides an effective method for contact force safety guarantees in soft robots.
limitations: Contact simulation capabilities (collision and friction with external rigid bodies or complex environments) are currently limited and remain an area for future extension.
Modifying robot topology (number of segments or strain basis order) triggers JAX recompilation, requiring specialized workflows when performing architectural search.
Supported actuation modes are currently limited to tendons and pneumatic chambers, with smart material actuators like DEAs and SMAs slated for future development.
